newsitem.title: UK: FTSE 100 dives on fears of post-budget rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FTSE 100 dives on fears of post-budget rate rise.

text.p: Britain's FTSE 100 share index plunged at the opening on Thursday on fears that interest rates would have to rise by at least a quarter point next week following a more lenient than expected budget, strategists said.
The index was 52.5 points off at 4,698.9 by 0745 GMT.
"Basically we are worried about base rates and the currency," said Dresdner Kleinwort Benson's Philip Isherwood.

"In the budget, whilst the Chancellor talked about coming down on demand, he didn't hit the consumer that hard and the reaction to that is that base rates will have to go up, probably next week, and by at least 25 basis points," said Isherwood.
Strategists said the market was factoring in as much as a half-point rate hike at the July 10 monetary meeting.
Gilts eased and sterling carried on upwards in early trading on Thursday with the prospect of higher rates.
The Chancellor (finance minister) Gordon Brown was still delivering his first budget at the London close on Wednesday.

The stock market gave an initial positive reaction, closing 23.1 points ahead at 4,751.4 with the most significant feature of the budget seen as the abolition of dividend tax relief which, although expected, was seen hitting shares as investors switched into gilts.
On further consideration the market took the effects of higher rates as the big negative with the budget seen as not fiscally tight enough to stave off demand sufficiently.
The Chancellor is seen as not having done enough to dampen buoyant consumer spending.

"The budget leaves the task of slowing the consumer boom to the Bank of England, meaning that interest rates are likely to rise by around 100 basis points over the remainder of the year," said Paribas strategists Paul Mortimer-Lee and Nick Parsons.
Some see rates as high at eight percent by the end of the year.
"The big question is not what happens next week but what happens over the remainder of the year," said Charterhouse group economist, Richard Jeffrey, who sees rates at eight percent by the year end.
"That will unnerve the City," he said.
"All it needs is one poor inflation number and the City will take fright. The mitigating factor at the moment is that inflation is low," Jeffrey said.
The effect of the budget varies sector by sector although in general stronger sterling will keep the pressure on exporters.
Utilities' share prices were mixed. Budget news that the windfall tax will be a net 4.8 billion stg - the lower end of 3-7 billion stg expectations - sent a wave of relief through the sector.
PowerGen rose 23p to 752-1/2p, National Power 31p to 565p, Centrica 4-1/2p to 80-1/2p, British Telecom 8p to 465-1/2p and Railtrack 20p to 652p.
